opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point for us was this observation that if you treat trained neural networks themselves as a data modality, you suddenly have a lot of interesting questions you can ask. Early on, most of the work on generating weights, things like hypernetworks, was done on very small models, a few thousand parameters, often on MNIST-scale problems. That's fine for proving a concept, but it doesn't tell you much about whether the idea holds up for the kinds of models people actually use.

The first thing we realized was that we needed the data. You can't learn a generative model over neural networks without a large, diverse population of trained networks. So we invested quite a bit of effort into building what we call model zoos: systematically trained collections of models across different architectures, datasets, initializations and hyperparameters, with the training trajectories recorded as well. That gave us a structured dataset where we could actually study the weight space rather than just looking at one model at a time.

The second piece was representation. Weights have a lot of structure. There are permutation symmetries, the layers are very different in size and role, and naively flattening everything into one long vector just doesn't scale. So we moved toward tokenizing the weights, breaking them into chunks at the neuron or layer level, and using transformer-based encoders to learn a latent representation of the model. We trained these in a self-supervised way, with reconstruction objectives plus contrastive objectives that use augmentations respecting those symmetries, like permuting neurons in a way that leaves the function unchanged.

Once you have a good latent space, generation becomes much more tractable. You can sample from that space, or fit a generative model on top of it, decode back into weights, and get networks that actually perform well, sometimes as a starting point that you then fine-tune much faster than training from scratch. And the tokenized, sequential view is what lets you scale: instead of needing to predict millions of parameters at once, you can handle them in windows, which is what allowed us to go from toy models toward larger architectures like ResNets and beyond.

So in short: build the data properly, respect the structure of weight space, and design the representation so it scales with model size. Those three things were really what moved it out of the toy regime for us.

r001.rationale: The response says the tokenized sequential view scales generation by handling parameters in windows instead of predicting millions of parameters at once, conveying windowed reconstruction rather than reconstructing the whole model at once.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that for a long time we were stuck exactly there, in toy land. The early work on hypernetworks and on generating weights with a model was beautiful conceptually, but what came out were tiny MLPs or small CNNs on MNIST, and if you tried to scale the same idea up it just fell apart. The core problem is that the weight space is enormous and it is full of symmetries. You can permute the neurons in a layer and get a functionally identical network with a completely different parameter vector, so a naive generative model is trying to learn a distribution that looks like noise.

Our first step was really to stop thinking about weights as a flat vector and start treating them as data with structure. We built what we call model zoos, which are populations of thousands of trained networks, same architecture, same task, different seeds, different hyperparameters. That gave us something to actually learn from instead of a handful of models. Then we spent a lot of time on representations of the weight space itself, so learning embeddings of the parameters that respect the permutation symmetries and the layer structure, rather than fighting them. Once you have a sensible embedding, you can do things like predict a model's accuracy or its generalization gap just from the weights, and that was the signal to us that the representation was capturing something real.

The generation part then became much more like what people do in other modalities. You learn a latent space over the zoo, you sample in it, and you decode back to weights. The key for moving beyond toys was doing this in a tokenized, layer-wise fashion so the model does not need to see the entire parameter vector at once. That let us go from a few thousand parameters to architectures like ResNets and eventually to pretrained transformers, where we generate or fine-tune weights for new tasks and get networks that are not just functional but competitive with training from scratch, sometimes after a short refinement step.

And I should say, a big part of the approach was humility about evaluation. It is very easy to generate a network that looks fine on the distribution you sampled from and is useless anywhere else. So we always ask whether the generated models transfer, whether they are diverse, and whether they are actually different from the models in the zoo rather than near copies. That discipline is honestly what kept us from fooling ourselves as we scaled up.

r001.rationale: The response says generation is tokenized and layer-wise, avoiding the full parameter vector at once, but does not describe reconstructing windows of the parameter sequence.

astra-6.text: The way I approached it was to ask what would make a generated network useful beyond a small demonstration. Producing a set of weights is one thing; producing weights that actually give you a functioning model is another. So the emphasis had to be on evaluating the generated networks on the task they were meant to solve, and then gradually increasing the complexity. Can you preserve performance as the networks get larger? Can you handle variation between networks? That shifts the focus from whether you can generate something that looks like a neural network to whether you can generate something you would actually use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating generated networks and gradually increasing complexity, but does not describe reconstructing windows of a model’s parameter sequence instead of the entire model at once.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the important step was to move from generating a small network that works on a toy problem to asking whether we could generate the parameters of a much larger network. That changes the problem quite a bit, because the weights are high-dimensional and there are dependencies between layers. You can’t simply generate each weight independently and expect a functioning model.

So we approached it as a representation-learning problem: can we learn a useful representation of neural networks themselves? If we can capture the structure of well-performing networks in a latent space, then we can explore that space and generate new candidates. The crucial test is whether those generated networks actually perform the task. Reconstructing weights is useful, but ultimately you have to put the weights back into a network and evaluate its behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating parameters for larger networks and learning a latent representation, but it does not describe reconstructing windows of the parameter sequence instead of the entire model at once.
